Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Lincoln Chafee]] was eligible to run for re-election to a second term but decided to retire. He had been elected as an [[independent candidate]] and became a Democrat in 2013.{{Cite web |title=Gov. Chafee Officially Joins Democratic Party {{!}} Campaign 2014 {{!}} WPRI.com |url=http://wpri.com/dpp/news/local_news/mcgowan/warwick-ri-gov-lincoln-chafee-officially-becomes-democrat |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130609054220/http://wpri.com/dpp/news/local_news/mcgowan/warwick-ri-gov-lincoln-chafee-officially-becomes-democrat |archive-date=2013-06-09 |access-date=2026-04-24 |website=WPRI TV |language=en-US}} In primary elections held on September 9, 2014, the Democrats nominated [[State treasurer|Rhode Island Treasurer]] [[Gina Raimondo]] and the Republicans nominated [[Cranston, Rhode Island|Cranston]] Mayor [[Allan Fung]]. Also on the ballot were [[Robert J. Healey]] of the [[Moderate Party of Rhode Island|Moderate Party]] and two [[Independent politician|Independent]] candidates. Raimondo won the election, becoming the first Democrat to be elected governor since [[Bruce Sundlun]] in [[1992 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|1992]], as Chafee had been elected as an independent [[2010 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|in 2010]]. Raimondo became the first female governor in Rhode Island history. Democrats won Newport County for the first time in a gubernatorial election since [[1998 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|1998]], and Bristol and Washington counties since [[1992 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|1992]]. ==Background== In the [[2010 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|2010 gubernatorial election]], Republican incumbent [[Donald Carcieri]] was term-limited and unable to seek a third term in office. The Republicans nominated businessman John Robitaille and the Democrats nominated State Treasurer [[Frank T. Caprio]]. Also contesting the election were [[Moderate Party of Rhode Island|Moderate Party]] nominee [[Ken Block (politician)|Ken Block]] and [[Lincoln Chafee]], who served as a Republican U.S. senator from 1999 to 2007. After losing a bid for re-election [[2006 United States Senate election in Rhode Island|in 2006]], Chafee left the Republican Party and became an Independent, running for governor as such. After a close three-way race between Chafee, Robitaille and Caprio, Chafee won the election with a plurality, taking 36% to Robitaille's 34%, Caprio's 23% and Block's 6%. After constant speculation during his term, Chafee officially joined the Democratic Party on May 30, 2013. He had previously indicated that he might run for re-election as an Independent or a Democrat.{{cite web|url=http://www.boston.com/news/local/rhode-island/2012/12/14/gov-chafee-open-running-for-term-dem/Q5g9thzMcZzorBrTmyOYuM/story.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130910052032/http://www.boston.com/news/local/rhode-island/2012/12/14/gov-chafee-open-running-for-term-dem/Q5g9thzMcZzorBrTmyOYuM/story.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 10, 2013|title=RI Gov. Chafee open to running for 2nd term as Dem|date=December 14, 2012|access-date=December 18, 2012|agency=[[Associated Press]]|publisher=[[Boston.com]]|first=David|last=Klepper}} In the face of low approval ratings, polling showing him trailing in both the Democratic primary and the general election, and with weak fundraising, Chafee announced on September 4, 2013, that he would not run for re-election.{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/the-fix/wp/2013/09/04/why-lincoln-chafees-decision-not-to-run-for-reelection-is-more-good-news-for-democrats/|title=Why Lincoln Chafee's decision not to run for reelection is more good news for Democrats|date=September 4, 2013|access-date=September 6, 2013|newspaper=The Washington Post|first=Sean|last=Sullivan}}{{cite web|url=http://firstread.nbcnews.com/_news/2013/09/04/20327881-gov-chafee-wont-run-for-a-second-term?lite|title=Gov. Chafee won't run for a second term|date=September 4, 2013|access-date=September 6, 2013|work=NBC News|first=Jessica|last=Taylor}} Chafee thus became just the fourth governor in the history of Rhode Island to decline to seek a second term, after [[Byron Diman]] in 1847, [[Royal C. Taft]] in 1889 and [[William S. Flynn]] in 1924.{{cite web|url=http://blog.lib.umn.edu/cspg/smartpolitics/2013/09/chafee_just_4th_rhode_island_g.php|title=Chafee Just 4th Rhode Island Governor Since 1790 to Pass On 2nd Term|date=September 6, 2013|access-date=September 6, 2013|work=Smart Politics|first=Eric|last=Ostermeier|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004070640/http://blog.lib.umn.edu/cspg/smartpolitics/2013/09/chafee_just_4th_rhode_island_g.php|archive-date=October 4, 2013|url-status=dead}} ==Democratic primary== Gina Raimondo, Treasurer of Rhode Island, and Angel Taveras, mayor of Providence, announced their campaigns in late 2013 and the race initially seemed to be between the more fiscally moderate Raimondo and the more progressive Taveras. However, the entry of Clay Pell, an Obama administration official and grandson of [[Claiborne Pell]], into the race complicated things. Unions who had criticized Raimondo for cutting pension benefits and investing in hedge funds during her tenure as Treasurer and for fundraising from Wall Street and national lobbyists were split on whether to back Taveras or Pell. A coalition of unions including firefighters, police, supermarket clerks, and city employees backed Taveras, whereas the powerful teachers' unions backed Pell, unimpressed with Taveras' support for [[charter school]]s. Raimondo drew support from non-union and private sector workers and some private sector unions including iron workers. Pell spent over $3.4 million of his own money and ran a positive campaign, but he was much criticized for his inexperience and lack of ties to Rhode Island. Taveras emphasised his background as the son of poor Dominican immigrants to appeal to Latino and working-class voters. All three candidates agreed not to seek the endorsement of the state Democratic Party. Ultimately, Taveras and Pell took an almost equal share of the vote as progressive Democrats split their vote between the two, allowing Raimondo to win with a plurality. Raimondo won 36 of the state's 39 municipalities. Taveras won [[Central Falls, Rhode Island|Central Falls]] and Pell won [[Burrillville, Rhode Island|Burrillville]] and [[Foster, Rhode Island|Foster]].{{cite
